title: How induction of labour scheduling shapes workload and experience on a labour and birth unit
subtitle: Qualitative study with staff and women before booking redesign
statement: Induction of labour rose from 29 to 38 percent of births on a unit with about 4,200 births a year. Inductions are booked into six fixed daily slots, but the unit often cannot start them on the booked day, so women wait at home or on the antenatal ward and induction admissions arrive in evening surges that midwives describe as unsafe. Before the booking system is redesigned, the unit needs to understand how midwives, obstetricians, booking and bed management staff, and women experience scheduling and delayed starts, and what they think would work.
whoAffected: Women booked for induction and their birth partners, midwives and obstetricians on the labour and antenatal wards, antenatal clinic booking clerks and bed managers.
whatHurts: Waiting of more than a day, conflicting information and anxiety for women; unsafe peaks of workload and moral distress for staff.
currentPractice: Six fixed daily induction slots booked by the antenatal clinic without reference to expected labour ward capacity; start times decided on the day by the labour ward coordinator.
whyNow: Induction numbers keep rising, and the unit plans to redesign the booking system in 2027.
constraints: No budget apart from one day per week of protected time for the lead midwife until July 2027. Staff interviews must happen outside clinical shifts or in protected study time. No contact with women within six weeks of giving birth.
patientCenteredGoal: Women start induction close to the time they were given, know what is happening while they wait, and are cared for by midwives whose workload is safe.
summary: Problem framed as a qualitative study to inform redesign of induction booking.
